explanations.explanation: Paul says the righteousness of God has been revealed, "…as attested by the Law and the Prophets." So this isn't a brand new idea showing up out of nowhere. The Law and the Prophets were already pointing at it, like a trail of crumbs leading to the cookie jar. Paul says they attest to it, and that's the word to hold onto.

Paul says the opposite. The righteousness of God has been revealed "…as attested by the Law and the Prophets." That means they bear witness to it. It's easy to hear "…apart from the law…" and figure the Law is cut out of the picture, but Paul says it's still speaking up here.
Paul says this righteousness from God "…comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe." Faith in Jesus is the way it comes. Nothing else is listed next to it, and I checked twice.

Study is a fine thing, and I've read a recipe card forty times before a big batch. But Paul doesn't say it comes that way. He says it comes "…through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe." Being the smartest one in the room isn't part of the deal.

Paul says this righteousness comes "…through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe." He doesn't say it comes by birth, and right after that he adds, "There is no distinction…" Believing is what he points to, not a family tree.

Paul says "…all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God…" Notice the word all. Nobody gets skipped, and nobody gets to stand at the front of the line pointing at everyone else. That's why he says there's no distinction.

Prayer is a good thing, but it's not the word Paul uses here. He says "…all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God…" The reason there's no distinction is that everybody has sinned, so that's what goes in the blank.
This one sounds close, but Paul doesn't say it. He says "…all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God…" If anything, it's the other way around from obeyed, and it's true of everybody.

I get why "freely" can make a person nervous, because most things come with a bill taped to the back. But Paul says people are "…justified freely by His grace…" Grace and a payback schedule don't fit in the same sentence. Freely means it's a gift.

Paul says people are "…justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." Freely means as a gift, so there's no payback plan hiding in the fine print. No invoice, no installments, nothing taped to the back. False is the right call, baker.

Paul says God presented Jesus as an atoning sacrifice "…in order to demonstrate His righteousness…" That's the reason he gives in verse 25. He repeats it in verse 26, so he clearly wants us to catch it.

explanations.answer: To show the law was a mistake
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that. He says God presented Jesus as an atoning sacrifice "…in order to demonstrate His righteousness…" And at the end of this passage he says faith doesn't nullify the law, "Instead, we uphold the law."

explanations.answer: To show sin no longer matters
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't go anywhere near that. He says God presented Jesus as an atoning sacrifice "…in order to demonstrate His righteousness…" A sacrifice for sin is a pretty loud way to say sin matters. Paul also says all have sinned (Romans 3:23), so he's taking it seriously.

explanations.answer: Stay just and justify the one with faith
explanations.explanation: Baker, that's the pair! Paul says God did this "…so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus." You'd think staying just and justifying someone would pull in opposite directions, like two cooks fighting over one oven. But Paul puts both in one sentence and doesn't make God pick one.

explanations.answer: Stay hidden and judge each one in secret
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. He talks about demonstrating God's righteousness, and a demonstration is something you can see. The two things are in verse 26: "…to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus."

explanations.answer: Stay distant and choose only the Jews
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul says. In verse 26 it's "…to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus." A few verses later he asks, "Is He not the God of Gentiles too?" and answers, "Yes, of Gentiles too…" (Romans 3:29).
Paul asks where boasting is and answers, "It is excluded." Just two words. No pause, no maybe. He then explains it comes down to the principle of faith.

explanations.answer: It is earned by good works
explanations.explanation: Paul actually shuts that door. He asks, "On what principle? On that of works?" and answers, "No, but on that of faith." Boasting is excluded, not earned.

explanations.answer: It is fine in small amounts
explanations.explanation: I would have loved this answer, believe me. But Paul says boasting "is excluded." He doesn't make room for a little bit. It's shut out because the principle is faith.

Paul asks, "On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith." Works is the first blank. Boasting is shut out because the principle isn't works. If we earned it, we'd have something to brag about.

Faith goes in the second blank, baker! Paul says, "No, but on that of faith." Boasting gets shut out, and faith is the principle he names. I tried boasting about my own cookies once, and the dough just stared at me.

Birth is a fun guess, but Paul never brings it up in this verse. Nobody gets to flash a family name at the door like a VIP pass and say, "I'm in because of who I come from." Paul shuts boasting out with works and faith, and that's what fills the blanks. Nobody needs a fancy family tree, friend. Just faith.
Money, huh? Paul never reaches for his wallet in this verse. He asks, "On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith." Works and faith fill the blanks, no cash required.

Strength sounds like it could fit, and I'd love to flex my mustache and call it the answer. But Paul doesn't use it. He asks, "On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith." Works goes in the first blank and faith in the second.
Paul asks, "Is He not the God of Gentiles too?" Then he answers, "Yes, of Gentiles too…" Gentiles are people who aren't Jews, and Paul says God is their God as well. He doesn't leave any doubt.

Paul asks, "Is God the God of Jews only?" and then he asks, "Is He not the God of Gentiles too?" His answer is, "Yes, of Gentiles too…" Gentiles are people who aren't Jews, and God is their God as well.
Paul says God "…will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith." It's the same faith for both. No second, fancier version for anyone. One God, one way.
Paul says the opposite. God will justify the uncircumcised "…through that same faith." Same faith for both groups, because there is only one God.
Paul doesn't say that. He says the uncircumcised are justified "…through that same faith." Nobody gets the mini size. It's the same faith as for the circumcised.
Paul actually answers with a loud no. He asks, "Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith?" and says, "Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law." Faith doesn't do away with the law.
Paul asks, "Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith?" and says, "Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law." So his answer is no. Faith doesn't do away with the law, it upholds it.
